comparison.summary: Same ordering rule; your solution uses a seenB flag instead of searching for the substring ba.
details: Your solution scans characters, sets seenB after a b, and returns false if a later character is a.
The existing TypeScript returns !s.includes('ba'); Python checks that "ba" is absent. These are equivalent because the input contains only a and b.
Both take O(n) time and O(1) extra space. No JavaScript implementation was saved.

solutions.title: Track whether b has appeared
solutions.approach: Scan from left to right and set seenB when the first b appears. If any later character is a, return false; otherwise all a characters come before all b characters.
solutions.walkthroughMarkdown:
#### 1. Initialize the saved example

Use `s = "abab"`. Set `seenB = false`. The variable remembers whether a `b` has appeared anywhere earlier in the scan.

#### 2. Visit characters until the code returns

**Index `0`, `char = "a"`.** Check `char === "b"`: false, so leave `seenB = false`. Next check `char === "a" && seenB`: the first part is true and the second part is false, so the whole condition is false. Do not return; advance to the next character.

**Index `1`, `char = "b"`.** Check `char === "b"`: true, so set `seenB = true`. Next check `char === "a" && seenB`: the first part is false, so `&&` stops without evaluating its second part. The condition is false. Do not return; advance to the next character.

**Index `2`, `char = "a"`.** Check `char === "b"`: false, so `seenB` stays true. Next check `char === "a" && seenB`: true and true gives true. Execute `return false` immediately.

#### 3. Explain the early result

The `b` at index `1` appears before the `a` at index `2`, which violates the required ordering. Index `3` is not visited, and the final `return true` is not reached on this input. The saved example returns **false**.

For comparison, the complete successful input `s = "ab"` follows two iterations: index `0` leaves `seenB = false` and does not return; index `1` sets `seenB = true` and does not return because the character is not `a`. No characters remain, so that call reaches `return true`.

At most `n` characters are visited, so time is `O(n)` and extra space is `O(1)`, where `n` is the string length.
solutions.intuition: A valid string has an initial run of a characters followed by a run of b characters; either run may be empty. The only forbidden event is seeing an a after a b. Remembering whether a b has appeared is enough—there is no need to count either character.
hints: What single ordering violation makes the answer false?
Once a b has appeared, every later character must also be b. Keep one boolean that records this transition.

pseudocode.concept: Reject the first a that appears after any b.
steps: Start with seenB set to false.
Scan the string from left to right.
When the current character is b, set seenB to true.
When the current character is a and seenB is true, return false immediately.
If the scan finishes without a violation, return true.

solutions.explanation:
1. Before the first b, any number of a characters is allowed. The flag remains false during that initial run.
2. Seeing b permanently sets the flag. Any later a now proves that at least one b occurs before an a, so the function can return false without examining the rest of the string.
3. If the loop finishes, no such pair exists. All a characters therefore precede all b characters, including strings containing only one of the two letters.

timeComplexityBreakdown.variables: n is the number of characters in the string.

phases.label: Visit at most n characters with constant work per character

timeComplexityBreakdown.note: An ordering violation can end the scan early, but a valid string requires reading all n characters. The worst-case bound is therefore linear.
